items.followUp: Define monatomic and polyatomic molecules. Give one example of each.

rubric.why: The defining feature of a diatomic molecule is that it contains two atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a diatomic molecule as consisting of two atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a diatomic molecule contains two atoms; the atoms may be the same or different elements.

rubric.why: The defining feature of a triatomic molecule is that it contains three atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a triatomic molecule as consisting of three atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a triatomic molecule contains three atoms; the atoms may be the same or different elements.

modelAnswer: A diatomic molecule consists of two atoms; for example, H₂.
A triatomic molecule consists of three atoms; for example, H₂O.

items.followUp: What is the difference between an element and a compound? Give one example of each.

rubric.why: A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout, and a valid example demonstrates the idea.
rubric.description: States that a homogeneous mixture is uniform throughout and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature together with a valid example.

rubric.why: A heterogeneous mixture is not uniform throughout, and its components may remain distinguishable.
rubric.description: States that a heterogeneous mixture is non-uniform and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature together with a valid example.

modelAnswer: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout; for example, salt solution.
A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition throughout; for example, sand and water.

items.followUp: Find the empirical formula and molecular mass of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆.

rubric.why: The subscripts in C₂H₄O₂ reduce to the simplest whole-number ratio 1:2:1.
rubric.description: Gives the empirical formula of acetic acid.
Calculates the molecular mass with a suitable unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 60 g mol⁻¹, 60 amu, or 60 u.

modelAnswer: Acetic acid has molecular formula C₂H₄O₂; dividing the subscripts by 2 gives the empirical formula CH₂O.

items.followUp: How many electrons can the M shell accommodate? Give an example of an element whose M shell contains electrons.

rubric.why: The maximum capacities of the K and L shells are 2 and 8 electrons, respectively.
rubric.description: States the electron capacities of both K and L shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for K = 2 and L = 8.

rubric.why: A correct electron arrangement illustrates the shell capacities in an atom.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of an electron arrangement using the K and L shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as oxygen (K=2, L=6) or sodium (K=2, L=8, M=1).

modelAnswer: The K shell can accommodate 2 electrons, and the L shell can accommodate 8 electrons.
For example, oxygen has the electron arrangement K=2, L=6.

items.followUp: Describe Rutherford’s nuclear model of the atom.

rubric.why: Thomson proposed that the atom was a sphere of positive charge.
rubric.description: Identifies the atom as a positively charged sphere.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the sphere as positively charged.

rubric.why: The electrons were pictured as embedded in the positive sphere, making the atom electrically neutral overall.
rubric.description: States that electrons are embedded or distributed within the sphere.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons are embedded in or distributed through the positive sphere.

modelAnswer: According to Thomson’s “Plum Pudding” theory, an atom is a sphere of positive charge.
Electrons are embedded in this sphere, so the atom as a whole is electrically neutral.

items.followUp: Why do outer electrons in an atom experience less attraction from the nucleus when inner shells are occupied?

rubric.why: Larger atoms generally contain more occupied inner shells between the nucleus and outer electrons.
rubric.description: Relates larger atomic size to having more shells or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the greater number of shells in larger atoms.

rubric.why: Inner electrons screen outer electrons from some of the nucleus’s attraction.
rubric.description: Explains that inner electrons shield outer electrons from nuclear attraction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the shielding or screening by inner electrons.

modelAnswer: Bigger atoms have more electron shells, with more inner electrons.
These inner electrons shield the outer electrons from the full attraction of the nucleus, producing a greater shielding effect.

items.followUp: State Newlands’ contribution to the classification of elements.

rubric.why: Dobereiner classified certain elements in groups of three called triads, whose members had similar properties.
rubric.description: States that Dobereiner grouped similar elements into triads.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the groups of three and their similar properties.

rubric.why: In a triad, the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the arithmetic mean of the other two.
rubric.description: States the relationship between the atomic masses in a triad.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the approximate mean relationship; a valid example such as Li, Na, K may also support the statement.

modelAnswer: Dobereiner arranged elements with similar properties in groups of three called triads.
In a triad, the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the arithmetic mean of the atomic masses of the other two; for example, Li, Na and K.

items.followUp: Define a single covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond involves sharing two pairs of electrons between atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a double covalent bond in terms of two shared electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two pairs of electrons are shared.

rubric.why: O₂ and CO₂ contain double covalent bonds.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a double covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example such as O₂ or CO₂.

modelAnswer: A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
For example, the two oxygen atoms in an O₂ molecule are joined by a double covalent bond (O=O).
